So this part of the yard is on the north side of the irrigation ditch I posted about before, and is watered by drip irrigation instead of directly from the ditch. The drip irrigation will eventually be run from water pumped out of the pond, but I need to run an electrical conduit to the pump and find a reliable way to pump water from the pond without sucking up fish. Also need to build a small pump house to keep the pump out of the elements.

This area gets a large amount of sun and was one of the first polyculture areas I cultivated. Each area will eventually be dominated by a large berry bush or shrub, with understories of annual vegetables, herbs, and pollinators that in some way aid each other. Basically the berm to the left and the berry berm I posted about before, will grow to several feet and create kind of a hedge maze feel to it as you walk down the middle path. I left an open area in the middle to eventually put a small stone bench in a few years. Looking out across the area between the south side of the house and the north side of the berry berm.

http://i.imgtc.com/G68KoFRJby.jpg

Honeyberry, surrounded by zlata radishes.

http://i.imgtc.com/yMLtWpViv7.jpg

Another honeyberry, with more radishes. Beets are just starting to pop up under the mulch to the left.

http://i.imgtc.com/q3keFo5Ap3.jpg

Taking advantage of the small size of the elderberries, greens (endive, lettuce, sorrel, and spinach) and herbs (cilantro, basil, and stevia) are growing within easy picking range. Small elderberries spaced along the irrigation line will eventually grow to over 5 foot high. To the right, on the south side, bergamot and phlox act as an attractant for pollinators and predatory wasps, with carrots planted as an understory.

http://i.imgtc.com/241Gxlfpkz.jpg

One of the three small elderberry bushes.

http://i.imgtc.com/NdoNNkm2yu.jpg

Candy phlox, bergamot, and carrot on the south side. Snow crocuses, now dormant, fill in the space between the phlox and the path to the right.

http://i.imgtc.com/OloiTe9P4W.jpg

The phlox will eventually fill this area to suppress weeds, and keep coming back every year.

http://i.imgtc.com/jhfzO2Fnxd.jpg

Dill, thriving off the stored heat from the rocks, is close to going to seed. A line of small lavender plants borders the rock garden and will eventually be transplanted to the other side of the house when they are large enough to not get trampled by foot traffic.

http://i.imgtc.com/YnKtmbzkJY.jpg

Another set of greens like those with the elderberries. There are small groupings like this throughout the garden, preventing disease or insects from easily spreading through the whole crop.

http://i.imgtc.com/RPvVBWkkGm.jpg

The rock garden, for plants that need a lot of drainage. Rock soapwort is to the left, starting to trail down the sides of the rocks. These will eventually spread and act as a low ground cover. Flemish poppies are slowly starting to send up flower stalks.

http://i.imgtc.com/1QFdwTTaqn.jpg

From the other side you can see the thai basil, sage, thyme, and rosemary.

https://i.imgtc.com/TOJEjFFuZT.jpg

Leeks are doing well off the stored heat from the rocks, and are finger thick by this point.

https://i.imgtc.com/gThxjSBbY5.jpg

Standing at the rock garden and looking east, we move into a nearly continually shaded area. Plants are slower growing, which allows me to plants things that normally would get out of control in sunnier locations. To the left is valerian, lovage, and lots of comfrey, with lots of wild violets in between. Left of that, around the base of the mulberry tree, are herbs (marjoram, catnip, and mint), followed by a row of small aronias. The aronias will eventually grow very large, extending the berry berm hedge along the length of the irrigation ditch. Radishes, carrots, and garlic are planted throughout the area.

https://i.imgtc.com/cUuQoP7uof.jpg

Around the base of the mulberry are climbing beans.

https://i.imgtc.com/7c2WEbtJn2.jpg

One of the aronias, already trying to produce fruit. These have been picked off so it focuses its energy on its root system. These were planted last November, and survived the winter with no protection beyond a thin layer of mulch.

https://i.imgtc.com/0PAsfPoSUk.jpg

https://i.imgtc.com/U5Uedotg0p.jpg

Around the base of the catalpa, with scarlet runner beans beginning to climb the trunk, and perennial sweet mace establishing itself along the path.

https://i.imgtc.com/DBv0zh3FUU.jpg

A small hugelkulture mound. Blackberries continue the hedge line started by the berry berm and aronias. Violets are doing well in the shade, as well as perennial hyssop arcado, lemon balm, and valerian. Small carrots are popping up in the spaces in between.

https://i.imgtc.com/RvOB015TZ9.jpg

Another hugelkulture mound next to the other one. Similar to the other one, except with another variety of hyssop, and the addition of verbena hastata.

https://i.imgtc.com/GZnQS9N1KC.jpg

Looking up at the canopy, pinyon pines, catalpa, and mulberry.
